Technology briefing

Conexus AI: the mathematics is real. The product claims need proof.

A San Francisco firm spun out of MIT category theory sells “mathematical proof” of data integrity, and has lately wrapped that idea around a suite of AI products. The published research is serious. The uniqueness, scale and customer-impact claims are not independently evidenced. And “Pegel from Google” is almost certainly Pregel — a celebrated system that does a different job.

Research Lab briefing · Public sources only · 12 November 2026

A note on “Pegel” This briefing treats “Pegel from Google” as Pregel, Google’s large-scale graph-processing system (Malewicz et al., SIGMOD 2010). Confidence in the name is high: no Google project called Pegel turned up, and Pregel is a one-letter omission from a well-known Google paper, itself named after the river in Königsberg. Confidence that this is a useful product comparison is low. Pregel computes iterative algorithms on huge graphs. Conexus integrates and migrates structured data under formal schema mappings. They are not substitutes. The mismatch is carried through the comparison below, and closer Google analogues — Cloud Data Fusion, the Knowledge Graph, F1 schema change — are noted where they matter.

The bottom line

A real formal contribution, wrapped in claims the public record does not yet support.

  1. The core technology is genuine. Categorical Query Language (CQL) treats database schemas as algebraic theories (or categories), instances as models (functors), and data migration as a triple of adjoint functors — Δ, Σ and Π — with a compile-time theorem prover that refuses to materialise an instance violating the stated constraints. That programme is peer-reviewed in the Journal of Functional Programming (2017), Theory and Applications of Categories (2017) and the Journal of Automated Reasoning (2022), and is implemented in a downloadable tool. The “proofs” are real — relative to the schemas and mappings a user writes.
  2. What is proprietary is narrower than the marketing. The distinctive engineered piece is a chase-based algorithm for left Kan extensions (the Σ migration), patented and benchmarked in JAR 2022 as about ten times faster than prior left-Kan algorithms the authors themselves implemented. Open-source CQL is the reference implementation, but its licence is BSD-3 only for non-commercial and “exploratory/evaluative commercial” use. The commercial layer, and a newer suite of AI products (English-language queries, legal-citation checking, “no hallucinations”), sit largely outside the peer-reviewed record.
  3. The dramatic claims are almost all vendor-only. NASA, the Department of Defense, an $8m discovery at Synchrony Financial, “300,000 databases” at Uber, and “$50m+” of oil-and-gas specification conflicts are not corroborated by independent public sources found for this briefing. What is independently documented: two NIST SBIR awards and a NIST success story; co-authored papers with NIST, Stanford, Uber and Chevron researchers; and four granted US patents (the company says five). Open-source CQL is described by its own site as “production-ready for single-node in-memory” workloads — in tension with “any volume.”
  4. Pregel is the wrong yardstick for capability. If the question is name-matching, Pregel is the answer. If the question is “is Conexus better at what Google does with data,” Pregel is a distributed graph engine from 2010, not a data-integration product. On published scale, Pregel wins easily. On formal guarantees for schema-mapped migration, Conexus is doing a job Pregel does not attempt. A fairer Google comparison would be Cloud Data Fusion or the Knowledge Graph — and even there, no head-to-head public benchmark exists.

What Conexus is and sells

Conexus AI presents itself as an MIT spin-out that applied category theory — “the mathematics of the 21st century,” in the company’s phrase — to enterprise data. The firm was founded around 2015 as Categorical Informatics in Cambridge, Massachusetts, with NIST SBIR funding, and now operates as Conexus AI, headquartered in San Francisco, with claimed offices in Washington, London and Riyadh.

The three founders are Eric Daimler (CEO), a Presidential Innovation Fellow at the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy in 2016–17, described by the company as “First AI Advisor in the White House”; Ryan Wisnesky (CTO), Stanford BS/MS, Harvard CS PhD, formerly IBM Research Almaden (Clio, Orchid, HIL) and a postdoc with Spivak at MIT; and David Spivak (chief scientist), formerly on the MIT mathematics faculty, author of two books on applied category theory, and the originator of the functorial data model.

The technical core is CQL (Categorical Query Language). In this model a schema is a finitely presented category (a graph plus path equations, later generalised to an algebraic theory); a database instance is a set-valued functor on that schema; and a schema mapping (a functor) induces three canonical migrations: Δ (projection, composition), Σ (left adjoint: a union-like, left Kan extension) and Π (right adjoint: a join-like extension). Integration of several sources is typically a colimit, or “universal warehouse”: given the overlaps the user declares, there is a unique (up to unique isomorphism) best-integrated schema and instance, from which a desired target can then be queried. CQL’s automated theorem prover checks, at compile time, that a program cannot produce an instance that violates the stated integrity constraints. The company and the open-source site also advertise “perfect provenance”: every output row carries a lineage.

CQL is not a database management system. The community site is explicit: it “neither stores nor updates data.” It is a language and IDE, written in Java, that can import and export via JDBC and CSV, and — in a 2021 company demo — generate code for Spark and Hadoop. The same site says it is “production-ready for single-node in-memory data processing workloads, such as integrating data for data science,” with scalability “similar to that of SQL and chase engines.”

What is for sale today

The current website is organised around six named capabilities. The first of these is the direct descendant of the research. The later ones extend the “mathematical proof” language into documents, English questions and large language models — a move that the paper inventory does not yet underwrite.

Migration Assurance

The core CQL pitch: integrate or migrate n sources with n mappings to a universal schema, not n(n−1) point-to-point maps, and prove that constraints survive. “Eleven sources, eleven mappings. Not 110.”

Project Integrity

Verify that construction or engineering specifications are complete and consistent before work starts. Marketed especially at bilingual (English/Arabic) Gulf mega-programmes. Closest paper: the Chevron-co-authored spreadsheet-integration preprint, and a 2026 building-lifecycle preprint.

Query Intelligence

“Ask questions in English. Get answers from your data. With proof.” Natural-language access to enterprise data, claimed to return a mathematical proof of correctness. No peer-reviewed paper in the inventory describes this end-to-end product.

Knowledge Amplification

A verified knowledge layer under an LLM. The page says “No hallucinations possible.” That sentence is a marketing claim, not a theorem in the published work.

Litigation Intelligence

A legal-citation verification engine, pitched at US Rule 11 and “MENA digital sovereignty.” Every citation classified Verified, Flagged, or Unable to Verify. No Conexus paper on legal citations was found.

Verify360

Continuous verification of integrity, lineage and consistency across a data estate, with “audit-ready” proofs. An operational wrapping of the core idea; no separate evaluation was found.

Sources: conexus.com/about; capabilities; categoricaldata.net; Wisnesky CV; NIST SBIR success story. The “first AI advisor” wording is the company’s; the documented role is a Presidential Innovation Fellowship at OSTP, 2016–17.

The proprietary edge: claims versus evidence

The interesting question is not whether category theory can describe databases — it can, and has been able to since at least Spivak’s 2012 paper — but whether Conexus’s implementation is meaningfully better than ordinary ETL, schema-mapping and data-exchange tools. Below, each marketing or technical claim is rated strong (peer-reviewed or independently documented, with a clear scope), weak (some supporting material, but narrow, self-reported, or in tension with other facts), or none (vendor assertion only, or contradicted by the public record). Click a card to expand. Ratings are this briefing’s, not the vendor’s.

A proof in CQL is a proof that a program is consistent with the schemas, mappings and constraints the user supplied. If those are wrong, the “mathematically certain” warehouse is a certain account of a wrong model. That is not a criticism of the mathematics. It is the right way to read every guarantee below.

Evidence ratings by this briefing, 12 November 2026, against the sources in §7. “Strong” is not a recommendation to buy; “none” is not a finding of falsehood. Several dollar and customer claims may be true and still, as of this date, publicly unverified.

Head-to-head with Google Pregel

Pregel is Google’s system for processing graphs with billions of vertices and trillions of edges. Programs are a sequence of “supersteps” in the Bulk Synchronous Parallel model: in each superstep every vertex, conceptually in parallel, reads messages sent in the previous step, updates its state, and sends messages that will be read in the next. The 2010 SIGMOD paper reports that implementing PageRank takes about 15 lines, and that the system had already been used internally on many applications. It is named after the Pregel river in Königsberg. Google has not sold Pregel as a cloud product; the open-source descendants are Apache Giraph and, in spirit, Spark GraphX.

Conexus does not do this. CQL does not “think like a vertex,” does not run BSP supersteps, and does not, on the public evidence, process billion-vertex graphs. What it does — formal, constraint-preserving migration between schemas — Pregel does not do. A comparison is still informative, because it shows what each system’s published evidence is actually evidence of.

Dimension Conexus / CQL Google Pregel
Problem Integrate, migrate and query structured data across heterogeneous schemas, with declared constraints and overlaps. Run iterative graph algorithms (PageRank, shortest paths, connected components, cuts, matchings) on very large graphs.
Computational model Category theory: schemas as categories or algebraic theories; instances as functors or algebras; migrations as adjoints Δ, Σ, Π; integration as a colimit; Σ implemented by a chase. Bulk Synchronous Parallel. Vertex-centric API: “think like a vertex.” Messages between supersteps; a master coordinates workers; checkpointing for faults.
Correctness offer Compile-time theorem proving that a program cannot materialise an instance violating user-specified constraints; migrated instances are universal (unique up to unique isomorphism) given the mapping. Proof is relative to those inputs. Synchronous supersteps make programs easier to reason about and free of the deadlocks typical of asynchronous systems. The vertex program’s meaning is the user’s responsibility. No schema-mapping or integrity layer.
Published scale Community site: “production-ready for single-node in-memory” work. JAR 2022: a MacBook Air benchmark, and the claim that the algorithm is “fast enough to support multi-gigabyte real-world use cases,” citing the 2019 materials-science paper. A 2021 company demo mentions Spark/Hadoop code generation and says whole enterprise databases “won’t fit” in CQL. No public cluster-scale benchmark was found. The 2010 paper and Google’s research blog: billions of vertices, trillions of edges, clusters of thousands of commodity machines. That figure is more than a decade old and is still of a different order from anything published for CQL.
What you can actually run Open-source CQL IDE (GitHub, 367 stars as of 12 November 2026) under a BSD-3 licence limited to non-commercial and exploratory commercial use; production commercial use requires a Conexus licence. Six named commercial capabilities on conexus.com. Internal Google system, not a Google Cloud SKU. Open implementations: Apache Giraph (the closest clone), and graph layers on other engines. Google Cloud Dataproc / Dataflow can run graph jobs, but that is not Pregel-the-paper.
Intellectual lineage Spivak’s functorial data model (2012); Wisnesky’s work on IBM Clio / Orchid / HIL; classical data-exchange and the chase (Fagin, Kolaitis, Miller, Popa and others). The JAR paper’s stated contribution is to compute left Kan extensions by the chase, about 10× faster than prior left-Kan algorithms in the authors’ Java implementations. Valiant’s BSP model; a reaction to the awkwardness of MapReduce for iterative graph algorithms. Hugely influential: Giraph, GraphX, GraphLab and a decade of “think like a vertex” research.
First landmark paper Spivak, “Functorial Data Migration,” Information and Computation, 2012; CQL itself in Schultz & Wisnesky, JFP, 2017. Company founded 2015. Malewicz et al., “Pregel: A System for Large-Scale Graph Processing,” SIGMOD 2010.
What it is not Not a graph-processing engine; not a DBMS (it does not store or update data); not, on public evidence, a drop-in at Google’s operational scale. Not a data-integration or schema-mapping system; not a theorem prover; not a product you can buy from Google under that name.

Sources: Malewicz et al., SIGMOD 2010, and Google’s Pregel blog post; categoricaldata.net; Schultz & Wisnesky, JFP 2017; Meyers, Spivak & Wisnesky, JAR 2022; CategoricalData/CQL README (licence) and GitHub API (star count, 12 November 2026); Conexus 2021 warehouse demo.

If the intent was a functional comparison

If “Pegel” was not a misspelling, or if the real question is how Conexus sits against Google as a data company, the closer analogues are:

  • Google Cloud Data Fusion (built on CDAP) — a commercial ETL and integration service. This is the product-category peer of Migration Assurance. Google publishes operational integration tooling; Conexus publishes formal guarantees. There is no public head-to-head.
  • Google Knowledge Graph — entity-centric integration at web scale. Algebraic Property Graphs (Shinavier, Wisnesky, Meyers) is Conexus’s closest intellectual neighbour, and grew out of formalising a toolkit at Uber, not at Google.
  • F1 online schema change (Google research, used in AdWords) — a formal protocol for evolving a live distributed schema without corruption. Adjacent problem, different mathematics, production evidence inside Google.

Wisnesky’s own earlier work at IBM on Clio, Orchid and HIL is a closer ancestor than any Google system. Clio was the classic schema-mapping tool. CQL is best read as a category-theoretic successor to that line, not as an answer to Pregel.

Questions to take into diligence

These are the gaps that a pilot, a reference call or a contract should close. None of them requires accepting or rejecting the mathematics.

1. Show the proof on our schemas.
Ask for a compile-time proof, and a failed proof, on a slice of your actual sources. Confirm what is being proved: consistency with your mappings, not correspondence with the world. Who writes the mappings, and what happens when they are wrong?
2. Name the production systems, with contacts.
NASA, the Department of Defense, Synchrony Financial, Uber and a “national oil company” appear on the company site. Ask which product ran, on what data volumes, for how long, and whether a named person will speak. The Uber paper describes formalising a toolkit developed at Uber; that is not the same as CQL processing 300,000 databases.
3. Open-source CQL versus the product you would buy.
What in Migration Assurance, Query Intelligence and the rest is the public CQL IDE, and what is closed? The GitHub licence does not grant ordinary commercial production use. Get the licence, the price, and the difference in writing.
4. Scale, in numbers, on hardware you recognise.
The public ceiling is “single-node in-memory” and “multi-gigabyte,” with a parenthetical Spark/Hadoop generator in a 2021 demo. Ask for the largest production instance (rows, gigabytes, wall-clock, machines) and whether the Spark path is in production. “Any volume” on the marketing pages should be reconciled with “they won’t fit” in the demo.
5. For the AI products: what is a theorem, and what is a model?
Query Intelligence (English in, “proof” out), Knowledge Amplification (“no hallucinations possible”) and Litigation Intelligence (Rule 11 citation checks) are not described in the peer-reviewed CQL papers. Ask for the formal boundary: which steps are checked by the theorem prover, and which are LLM or retrieval. “No hallucinations possible” should be treated as a claim to be demonstrated, or withdrawn.
6. Why is “11 mappings, not 110” better than a canonical model?
Ordinary hub-and-spoke warehouses also write n maps to a common schema. The mathematical difference is that CQL’s integrated schema is a universal construction, uniquely determined by the overlaps. Ask to see that uniqueness used in practice — for example, a gap analysis against a desired warehouse — not just a count of arrows.
7. Reconcile “five patents” with four grants.
Justia lists four granted US patents assigned to Conexus ai, Inc., including a 2023 continuation of the 2022 chase patent. A further continuation (US 18/212,320, published as US20240119034A1) was filed in 2023; this briefing did not confirm a fifth grant. Ask for the fifth number.
8. How were the dollar figures computed?
“$8 million in hidden data relationships” at Synchrony, and “$50m+ in specification conflicts” in oil and gas, are vendor figures with no public methodology. Ask for the counterfactual, the period, and whether the customer will confirm them. The Chevron-co-authored spreadsheet paper is a real case study of two MASP calculation sheets; it does not contain a $50m figure.
9. Chase cost and failure modes.
The chase can fail, or fail to terminate, on some theories; JAR 2022 discusses completeness for cartesian theories under fairness assumptions, and an “unfailing” variant. Ask when CQL’s prover or chase times out, what the user sees, and how often that happens on realistic constraints. Category theory does not make an undecidable problem decidable in general; the JFP paper is candid that word problems are not always computable.
10. Who still knows the mathematics, if the founders are busy?
The published work is concentrated on Wisnesky, Spivak, and a small group of co-authors (Schultz, Meyers, Shinavier, and others). For a multi-year deployment, ask about the delivery team, documentation, and what happens when a mapping needs a category theorist.
